title: Rattan Singh Bhangu
hook: his Panth Prakash told the Khalsa's hard century in verse

segments.voice: Yesterday, how we know this: Sikh chroniclers, Persian records, and memory. Your line was how do we know. Did you ask your elder? Today, one of those chroniclers, by name. Day eight hundred seventy-six.

A Sikh sits down to write. Not in prose. In verse, line after line that can be read aloud and remembered. He has the stories his family told him, the stories of the riders and the forests, the great killing, the temple blown up and rebuilt. Some of them are about his own family. And, by his own account, he has a reason to write: outsiders are asking about the Sikhs, and he wants the Sikh side told by a Sikh. Today: Rattan Singh Bhangu.
screen: `A SIKH WRITES IN VERSE.` → `STORIES HIS FAMILY TOLD HIM.` → `THE SIKH SIDE, TOLD BY A SIKH.`

segments.voice: First, the book. It's called Panth Prakash. Panth is the path, and the word Sikhs use for the whole community. Prakash is light, the shining of something into view. So the title promises to bring the Panth into the light. Second, why he wrote it. Bhangu says that a British officer was collecting accounts of Sikh history, and that he heard the Sikhs described by people who didn't know them. So he set out to tell it from inside. That's a choice worth noticing. He didn't write an angry reply. He wrote the long story, with names, places and family memory, so it would be there for anyone who asked. Third, his family is in it. Bhangu traces his line to Mehtab Singh, one of the riders remembered for punishing the man who had turned the Harmandir into a place of drinking and dancing. So when he tells the hard century, he isn't telling strangers' stories. He's telling his own family's world. Fourth, how to read him. Because he wrote later, from memory and family tradition, historians read him carefully, setting him beside other sources. That's yesterday's lesson in action. And yet several stories on this path in recent weeks, Kapur Singh fanning the sangat, the boy Jassa Singh singing, the shaheedi bunga, are told in the forms Sikhs know through tellings like his. When this path says tradition says, Bhangu is one of the voices in that tradition. The chronicler.
screen: `PANTH PRAKASH: THE PATH BROUGHT TO LIGHT.` · `WRITTEN SO THE SIKH SIDE WAS TOLD.` · `HIS OWN FAMILY IN THE STORY.` · `READ CAREFULLY, AND STILL TREASURED.` · then, large: `THE CHRONICLER.`

segments.voice: For this sit, read one line of history. It can be anything: a sentence from a history book, a plaque on a building, an inscription on a gravestone, an old letter, the first line of a page about where your family came from. Find it now, or recall one you know. Read it slowly, once. Then put it down and breathe. Ask: who wrote this, and from where were they standing? Let the question sit with you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhangu. The Sikh chronicler whose Panth Prakash told the Khalsa's hard century in verse, from family memory, so the Sikh side would be told. Today's word.
Your line: the chronicler. Today, write down one family story you've heard, just a few lines, with who told it to you, so it's there for someone who asks. Day eight hundred seventy-six.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old history book.
what it means: a Sikh's verse chronicle of the hard century, written from family memory so the Sikh side would be told.
what a scholar hears: an insider source, written well after many of the events, valued for names and memory and read critically beside Persian and other accounts.

notes: Bhangu's stated reason for writing (a British officer, commonly identified as Captain Murray at Ludhiana, collecting accounts of Sikh history): confirm it is in his introduction and the framing 'heard the Sikhs described by people who didn't know them'.
Bhangu's descent from Mehtab Singh (who with Sukha Singh killed Massa Ranghar for desecrating the Harmandir): confirm 'grandfather' and the description; 'one of the two riders' is a count, confirm.
Panth as 'path, the whole community' and Prakash as 'light': confirm glosses.
The index gives 1841 for the finishing; no year is given in the voice.
'several stories on this path in recent weeks ... are told in the forms Sikhs know through tellings like his' is general; confirm or soften.
Gurmukhi ਪੰਥ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ and pronunciation; confirm.
Editor: changed 'a reason to hurry' (not in the source) to 'a reason to write'.
Audit: read in full; no changes. Keeper: Bhangu's account names the officer as Captain Murray and the outside informant as Bute Shah; the voice keeps both unnamed.
